```{r}
#| label: tbl-area
#| echo: true
#| tbl-cap: "Forest and susceptible forest in the four test regions and in Alaska, from the 1 km map. Forest is the area of 10 m cells with canopy height of 5 m or more; susceptible forest is the forest whose pre-outbreak VV level reached the strip's threshold, and tall forest the forest whose canopy height reached the strip's height threshold. Scenes is the median number of Sentinel-1 scenes behind a forest cell."
fmt_tbl(data.frame(Region = c(region_names[state_area$region[state_area$region != "alaska"]], "Alaska"), `Forest (km²)` = format(round(state_area$forest_km2), big.mark = " "), `Susceptible (km²)` = format(round(state_area$susceptible_km2), big.mark = " "),
  `Susceptible (%)` = sprintf("%.0f", 100 * state_area$susceptible_km2 / state_area$forest_km2), `Tall (km²)` = format(round(state_area$tall_km2), big.mark = " "), Scenes = round(state_area$scenes), check.names = FALSE))
```

## Regional validation

Against the aerial detection survey, the radar map ranked attacked above unattacked forest with an area under the curve of `r sprintf("%.2f", region_auc["AUC_VV", "kenai"])` on the Kenai Peninsula and `r sprintf("%.2f", region_auc["AUC_VV", "matsu"])` in the Matanuska-Susitna Borough, where the attacked stands were `r sprintf("%.1f", region_auc["VV_dead", "matsu"] - region_auc["VV_living", "matsu"])` dB brighter and `r sprintf("%.1f", region_auc["height_dead", "matsu"] - region_auc["height_living", "matsu"])` m taller than the unattacked. In the Copper River basin, where the survey had recorded damage only since 2022, it gave `r sprintf("%.2f", region_auc["AUC_VV", "copper"])`, and both classes were darker (`r sprintf("%.1f", region_auc["VV_dead", "copper"])` against `r sprintf("%.1f", region_auc["VV_living", "copper"])` dB) and shorter (`r sprintf("%.1f", region_auc["height_dead", "copper"])` against `r sprintf("%.1f", region_auc["height_living", "copper"])` m) than in the two southern regions. In the Interior, it gave `r sprintf("%.2f", region_auc["AUC_VV", "interior"])`. The `r format(region_auc["dead", "interior"], big.mark = " ")` dead cells of that sample all lay between `r sprintf("%.1f", min(pooled_region$interior$lat[!is.na(pooled_region$interior$year)]))`° N and `r sprintf("%.1f", max(pooled_region$interior$lat[!is.na(pooled_region$interior$year)]))`° N along the Nenana River, and `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * mean(pooled_region$interior$year[!is.na(pooled_region$interior$year)] >= 2021))` per cent of them were first recorded in 2021 or later. The height map gave `r sprintf("%.2f", region_auc["AUC_height", "kenai"])`, `r sprintf("%.2f", region_auc["AUC_height", "matsu"])`, `r sprintf("%.2f", region_auc["AUC_height", "copper"])`, and `r sprintf("%.2f", region_auc["AUC_height", "interior"])` in the same four regions, respectively (@tbl-regions). In the Matanuska-Susitna Borough, the nine single sources scored from `r sprintf("%.2f", min(matsu["AUC", ]))` to `r sprintf("%.2f", max(matsu["AUC", ]))` against the same label, the highest being `r ms_names[colnames(matsu)[which.max(matsu["AUC", ])]]`. Limiting the dead cells to polygons of 20 per cent mortality or more changed nothing, `r sprintf("%.2f", min(matsu["AUC_severe", ]))` to `r sprintf("%.2f", max(matsu["AUC_severe", ]))`, so the survey label set the ceiling. The stands the survey first recorded in 2016 and 2017 were the tallest, `r sprintf("%.1f", ms_year["2016", "height_eth"])` and `r sprintf("%.1f", ms_year["2017", "height_eth"])` m on ETH Zurich height, and those first recorded in 2024 the shortest, `r sprintf("%.1f", ms_year["2024", "height_eth"])` m, with Spearman's rho between year and height of `r sprintf("%.2f", ms_trend["height_eth"])` over cohorts of `r format(min(ms_year_n), big.mark = " ")` to `r format(max(ms_year_n), big.mark = " ")` cells.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-regions
#| echo: true
#| tbl-cap: "The statewide product against the aerial detection survey in four regions. Dead cells lay inside a spruce beetle polygon on white spruce of 2016 to 2024; living cells were forest the surveyors flew over, never inside a spruce beetle polygon of any year, within 10 km of one. AUC is the area under the curve for ranking dead above living; the two shares are the cells of each class the strip's VV threshold called susceptible; rho is Spearman's correlation between the year a dead cell was first recorded and its canopy height."
rt <- data.frame(Region = region_names[colnames(region_auc)], Dead = format(region_auc["dead", ], big.mark = " "), Living = format(region_auc["living", ], big.mark = " "),
  `AUC, VV` = sprintf("%.2f", region_auc["AUC_VV", ]), `AUC, height` = sprintf("%.2f", region_auc["AUC_height", ]), `VV dead (dB)` = sprintf("%.1f", region_auc["VV_dead", ]), `VV living (dB)` = sprintf("%.1f", region_auc["VV_living", ]),
  `Susceptible dead (%)` = sprintf("%.0f", 100 * region_auc["above_dead", ]), `Susceptible living (%)` = sprintf("%.0f", 100 * region_auc["above_living", ]), `rho year, height` = ifelse(is.na(region_auc["rho_year_height", ]), "", sprintf("%.2f", region_auc["rho_year_height", ])), check.names = FALSE)
fmt_tbl(rt)
```

## Ground plots

On the ground, the trees that died were the large ones. In the Matanuska-Susitna Borough, on the `r fia_ground["both", "matsu"]` plots holding both live and dead white spruce, the dead trees averaged `r sprintf("%.1f", fia_ground["dia_dead", "matsu"])` cm in diameter and `r sprintf("%.1f", fia_ground["ht_dead", "matsu"])` m in height against `r sprintf("%.1f", fia_ground["dia_live", "matsu"])` cm and `r sprintf("%.1f", fia_ground["ht_live", "matsu"])` m for the live trees [paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test, V = `r format(fia_ground["V_dia", "matsu"], big.mark = " ")`, `r pfmt(fia_ground["p_dia", "matsu"])` for diameter and V = `r format(fia_ground["V_ht", "matsu"], big.mark = " ")`, `r pfmt(fia_ground["p_ht", "matsu"])` for height]. Across the `r fia_ground["plots", "matsu"]` plots, the share of white spruce basal area standing dead rose with the height of the tallest tree [Spearman's rho `r sprintf("%.2f", fia_ground["rho_share_ht", "matsu"])`], which ranked the `r fia_ground["half_dead", "matsu"]` plots with at least half their basal area dead with an area under the curve of `r sprintf("%.2f", fia_ground["AUC_ht_half", "matsu"])`. On the Kenai Peninsula, the dead trees on the `r fia_ground["both", "kenai"]` plots holding both were again the larger, `r sprintf("%.1f", fia_ground["dia_dead", "kenai"])` cm and `r sprintf("%.1f", fia_ground["ht_dead", "kenai"])` m against `r sprintf("%.1f", fia_ground["dia_live", "kenai"])` cm and `r sprintf("%.1f", fia_ground["ht_live", "kenai"])` m for the live trees [V = `r format(fia_ground["V_dia", "kenai"], big.mark = " ")`, `r pfmt(fia_ground["p_dia", "kenai"])` and V = `r format(fia_ground["V_ht", "kenai"], big.mark = " ")`, `r pfmt(fia_ground["p_ht", "kenai"])`]. In the Copper River basin, the dead trees were `r sprintf("%.1f", fia_ground["dia_dead", "copper"])` cm in diameter against `r sprintf("%.1f", fia_ground["dia_live", "copper"])` cm on `r fia_ground["both", "copper"]` plots [V = `r format(fia_ground["V_dia", "copper"], big.mark = " ")`, `r pfmt(fia_ground["p_dia", "copper"])`], with no difference in height [V = `r format(fia_ground["V_ht", "copper"], big.mark = " ")`, `r pfmt(fia_ground["p_ht", "copper"])`]. On the Interior plots, the dead white spruce on `r fia_ground["both", "interior"]` plots holding both were no thicker than the live ones, `r sprintf("%.1f", fia_ground["dia_dead", "interior"])` against `r sprintf("%.1f", fia_ground["dia_live", "interior"])` cm [V = `r format(fia_ground["V_dia", "interior"], big.mark = " ")`, `r pfmt(fia_ground["p_dia", "interior"])`], and were shorter, `r sprintf("%.1f", fia_ground["ht_dead", "interior"])` against `r sprintf("%.1f", fia_ground["ht_live", "interior"])` m [V = `r format(fia_ground["V_ht", "interior"], big.mark = " ")`, `r pfmt(fia_ground["p_ht", "interior"])`]. The ETH Zurich canopy height around a plot's published coordinate ranked the half-dead plots at `r sprintf("%.2f", fia_remote["eth.AUC_half", "matsu"])` in the Matanuska-Susitna Borough, against `r sprintf("%.2f", fia_ground["AUC_ht_half", "matsu"])` for the plot's own tallest tree.

# Discussion

Over the Susitna valley label areas of @Zwieback_2024, the Sentinel-1 VV level of October 2014 to December 2016 ranked the stands the outbreak would kill above those it left alive, while the change through the outbreak in the same cells ranked nothing, so the first hypothesis was supported against the best ground truth this outbreak has, and what the level validated was a measurement of the stand before the outbreak, not a detection of mortality. The product's rank correlation with the ETH Zurich height over the forest was `r sprintf("%.2f", pooled_strip["rho_height"])`, so the radar level measured stand height and the map is a map of tall stands, and height, the C-band level, and L-band HV each ranked the cells in the direction the review expected.

## Stand height

That the tall stands died is the oldest finding in the spruce beetle literature. On the Kenai Peninsula, 'Mortality was greatest in the larger diameter classes during the early part of the infestation' [@Werner_1983, p. 96], in the Copper River basin, 'Mortality increased with increasing DBH and decreasing BAI' [@Doak_2004, p. 810], that is with larger diameter and slower growth, and the Forest Service synthesis reduced the plot studies to the rule that 'Spruce beetles preferentially attack and kill large diameter trees that have been growing slowly at breast height' [@Hard_1985b, p. 7]. The present study found the rule at the scale of the stand, from free radar and canopy height data with no beetle in the predictor, and the inventory plots confirmed it in the same decade, in that the dead white spruce stood `r sprintf("%.1f", fia_ground["dia_dead", "matsu"] - fia_ground["dia_live", "matsu"])` cm thicker and `r sprintf("%.1f", fia_ground["ht_dead", "matsu"] - fia_ground["ht_live", "matsu"])` m taller than the live trees beside them in the Matanuska-Susitna Borough, while on the Interior plots measured before the outbreak's front arrived the dead trees were no larger, so the size effect belongs to the beetle. The qualification of @Hard_1983 [p. 678], that diameter mattered 'unless large diameter was coupled with slower than average radial growth in the last 5 years', is one the map does not include, because none of the measures here records growth, and height alone ranked the strip's stands at `r sprintf("%.2f", struct["AUC", "height_eth"])` without it. The order of attack was the same as on the White River [@Schmid_1976, p. 2], in that the stands the survey recorded first in the Matanuska-Susitna Borough, in 2016 and 2017, were the tallest and each year's new stands were shorter through to 2024. The contrast was present inside each LANDFIRE class with enough cells, so it was a contrast between tall and short stands of the same cover and not between host and non-host.

## Hazard ratings

The second hypothesis applied that finding to the hazard rating, which since @Schmid_1976 [p. 1] has scored stands 'on the basis of physiographic location, tree diameter, basal area, and percentage of spruce in the canopy'. Those ratings take their diameter, basal area, and spruce share from a cruise, and the thresholds now in use [@Fettig_2026, p. 8] have never been applied to the forest of a state. The map gives the hazard part of such a rating at 90 m across `r format(round(state_area$forest_km2[state_area$region == "alaska"]), big.mark = " ")` km² of forest from free data. Of that forest, `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * state_area$susceptible_km2[state_area$region == "alaska"] / state_area$forest_km2[state_area$region == "alaska"])` per cent lay at or above the threshold that separated the killed strip stands from the spared, from `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * min(with(state_area[state_area$region != "alaska", ], susceptible_km2 / forest_km2)))` per cent in the Interior to `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * max(with(state_area[state_area$region != "alaska", ], susceptible_km2 / forest_km2)))` per cent on the Kenai Peninsula (@tbl-area). It is hazard and not risk, in the distinction @Reynolds_1994 drew when a panel of experts set stand hazard and windthrown trees as 'the two most important factors determining risk of a spruce beetle outbreak', because the map includes no windthrow, no beetle population, and no spruce share. A tall birch or aspen stand therefore scores as a tall spruce stand would, and a manager reads the map with the stand map in hand. What it directs is the prevention @Hard_1985b [p. 2] prescribed, 'Mark all spruce trees 14 inches (36 cm) or larger in diameter for removal regardless of growth rate', before the beetle arrives.

## Aerial surveys

Against the aerial detection survey, the map ranked attacked above unattacked forest at `r sprintf("%.2f", region_auc["AUC_VV", "kenai"])` on the Kenai Peninsula and `r sprintf("%.2f", region_auc["AUC_VV", "matsu"])` in the Matanuska-Susitna Borough. In the borough, every one of nine sources scored between `r sprintf("%.2f", min(matsu["AUC", ]))` and `r sprintf("%.2f", max(matsu["AUC", ]))` against the survey label, where the crown map had scored them at `r sprintf("%.2f", struct["AUC", "VV65_pre"])` to `r sprintf("%.2f", struct["AUC", "height_eth"])`. The survey is drawn from an aircraft at a scale at which a polygon of 2 per cent mortality is mostly living forest, and restricting the dead cells to polygons of 20 per cent mortality or more changed nothing. The ceiling is therefore the label's and the regional numbers are a lower bound on the map's skill. In the Copper River basin, the radar level failed where the height map did not, `r sprintf("%.2f", region_auc["AUC_VV", "copper"])` against `r sprintf("%.2f", region_auc["AUC_height", "copper"])`, because the attacked stands there were `r sprintf("%.1f", region_auc["height_dead", "copper"])` m tall against `r sprintf("%.1f", region_auc["height_dead", "matsu"])` m in the Matanuska-Susitna Borough and both classes averaged near `r sprintf("%.0f", region_auc["VV_living", "copper"])` dB. The radar map is therefore validated for the Kenai Peninsula and the Susitna lowlands, and the height map is the product for the Copper River basin, the narrowing of extent the design allowed for. In the Interior, the map scored `r sprintf("%.2f", region_auc["AUC_VV", "interior"])` at the front of the outbreak along the Nenana River, where `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * mean(pooled_region$interior$year[!is.na(pooled_region$interior$year)] >= 2021))` per cent of the recorded cells date from 2021 or later and the polygons contain stands the beetle has entered and not yet killed through.

## Limitations

The crown labels and severity map are one image of one valley on one date, and the threshold was set on that valley, so a region whose stands are taller or shorter will have more or fewer cells above it than the beetle will take. The ETH Zurich height is a 2020 model whose estimates 'saturate around 25 to 30 m' [@Lang_2023, p. 1779], just above the mean `r sprintf("%.1f", struct["dead", "height_eth"])` m of the strip's dead stands. The GLO-30 and ArcticDEM surfaces, the 2007 to 2010 PALSAR mosaic, and the 2014 to 2016 radar predate the outbreak and gave the same ranking. The pooling of orbits depends on one fitted fall of backscatter with incidence angle, `r sprintf("%.3f", angle_slope)` dB per degree, and on `r min(state_area$scenes[state_area$region != "alaska"])` to `r max(state_area$scenes[state_area$region != "alaska"])` scenes behind a forest cell in the four regions. Crown-scale detection in Alaska needs airborne hyperspectral and lidar data to reach '78% accuracy for all three health statuses' [@Cessna_2021], and Landsat detects the outbreak only above a severity of 0.1 [@Zwieback_2024]. The map offered here detects no outbreak at all, and claims only to say, before one arrives, where it will go.

# Conclusion

Validated against the crown labels and severity map of @Zwieback_2024, the pre-outbreak Sentinel-1 level and three independent canopy heights ranked the stands the spruce beetle killed in the Susitna valley above those it spared, the finding the plot studies have reported since 1954 at the scale of the tree, found here at the scale of the stand with no beetle in the predictor. Pooled across every scene over Alaska, the level gave a 90 m map of susceptible stands that ranked attacked above unattacked forest on the Kenai Peninsula and in the Susitna lowlands, where the inventory plots confirmed it on the ground, and failed in the open woodland of the Copper River basin, where the height map ranked them instead. The two maps give the hazard part of a stand rating with no cruise, and show forest managers which stands to protect first in the next outbreak.

# Data availability statement

Every input was public and was read by the code shown in this manuscript, except the severity map of Zwieback (2023), which carries no declared licence and was used for validation only. The crown labels of @Zwieback_2024 came from Zenodo [@Zwieback_2024_data] under the licence given in the code, the satellite, terrain, vegetation, and boundary layers were read in Google Earth Engine under the asset names given in the code, the aerial detection survey and the Forest Inventory and Analysis tables came from the United States Forest Service, and the conifer top cover from the Oak Ridge National Laboratory Distributed Active Archive Center. The 90 m statewide map is held as the Earth Engine asset named in the code. The sampled cells, the screening table of the literature review and the tables and figures are held with the manuscript in the same repository, and every number in the text is computed from them at render time.
